read: full: abstract, sections 1-6 and appendices A-C, E-F (pp. 1-17, 20-21); appendix D example solutions (pp. 18-19) have no text layer; references skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2110.14168v2, 18 Nov 2021 (p1 margin); the text shows no venue
what_it_is: GSM8K is a set of 8.5K grade-school math word problems written by human problem writers (Upwork contractors, then Surge AI), split 7.5K train / 1K test, each needing 2 to 8 steps of elementary arithmetic and each paired with the writer's natural-language solution (p3, p15). The paper's main contribution is a method: verifiers trained on final-answer correctness that rerank 100 sampled solutions, compared with plain fine-tuning of GPT-3 models from 3B to 175B (p5-8). Performance is the correctness of the final answer (p5).
size: 8.5K problems (7.5K train, 1K test) (p3); GPT-3 family fine-tuned at 3B, 6B, 12B and 175B (p5-6)
source_of_items: crowd-written by contractors (Upwork, then Surge AI); writers could start from seed questions generated by few-shot GPT-3 175B (p15)
has_gold_traces: yes: each problem has the writer's natural-language solution (p2, p3) with calculator annotations added automatically (p17); used for training, not to score model steps
evaluation: final answer: a single low-temperature sample is checked for the correct final answer; test@N over N samples (p5, p7); verifier reranking uses labels set only by final-answer correctness (p5, p7)
human_validation: items only: workers re-solved every problem; disagreements were repaired or discarded; a second check on a subset left 1.7% of problems with disagreements, the authors' estimate of problems with breaking errors or ambiguities (p15; 'less than 2 percent', p3). No validation of the scorer.
contamination_measures: none for the test set; writers were told not to reuse problem settings or templates, enforced with pairwise-similarity feedback (p15), which is a diversity measure

engtrace_use.sentence: S-M1 (L155-161): 'In mathematics, benchmarks ranging from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) to HardMath (Fan et al., 2024), Putnam-Axiom (Gulati et al., 2024), and GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al., 2024) rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability.'
engtrace_use.explanation: Citing GSM8K as a mathematics benchmark is right, but the characterisation is loose for this paper. GSM8K's problems are everyday word problems solved with 'elementary calculations using basic arithmetic operations', and 'A bright middle school student should be able to solve every problem' (p3); the authors stress 'the conceptual simplicity of this problem distribution' (p1), present the data as 'useful for probing the informal reasoning ability' of models (p2), and note that some problems need background knowledge such as the number of days in a week (p4). 'Abstract logical deduction' does not describe that, and 'rigorously' overstates a set with an estimated 1.7% of problems still disputed (p15) that is scored on the final answer alone (p5). 'Reasoning stability' is not tested here; it is GSM-Symbolic's contribution, built on GSM8K. The sentence also passes over the point most relevant to EngTrace: the authors state that with final-answer labels 'some solutions will reach the correct final answer using flawed reasoning, leading to false positives' (p7).

suggested_wording: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) pairs 8.5K human-written grade-school word problems with natural-language solutions but scores only the final answer, and its authors note that a correct final answer can rest on flawed reasoning.
facts_to_cite: 8.5K grade-school math word problems written by human problem writers, split into 7.5K training and 1K test problems; each takes 2 to 8 steps of basic arithmetic (p3).
Every problem comes with a natural-language solution written by the problem writer (p2, p3); the calculator annotations in the solutions were generated automatically (p17).
Models are scored on the final answer of a single low-temperature sample (p5).

Verifiers are trained on labels determined 'solely by whether or not the solution reached the correct final answer' (p5), and 'some solutions will reach the correct final answer using flawed reasoning, leading to false positives' (p7).
Workers re-solved all problems; after repairs, 1.7% of a re-checked subset still drew disagreement, the authors' estimate of problems with breaking errors (p15).
The authors deliberately avoided problems 'drawn from the same linguistic template or differ only in superficial details' (p3).
The token-level verifier, trained on outcome labels, 'can be viewed as a token-level value function' (p9).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-step quantitative problems with a worked reference solution for every item (p3), i.e. a gold trace in form. Lacks: generated instances (static, and deliberately anti-template, p3); step-level evaluation (final answer only, p5); engineering domain (grade-school arithmetic); expert validation of the evaluator (none; items checked only by crowd re-solving, p15). Its outcome-supervised verifiers (p5, p9) are the outcome-reward baseline that process supervision is defined against, so it can also be cited in the planned process-supervision paragraph.
notes: The reference entry (arXiv 2110.14168) matches the text, and its authors agree with the arXiv record (citation_context_map C-S). Karl Cobbe is also an author of Lightman et al. (2023). GSM8K is the static source of GSM-Symbolic's 100 templates (Mirzadeh et al., p4), so the two can be described together as a static set and its templated variants. The p7 sentence on false positives is a quotable motivation for step-level verification.
